title: 1 Chronicles
subtitle: Israel's story retold around David and the Temple
lead: 1 Chronicles tells Israel's story a second time. It begins with Adam and nine chapters of family lists that run through the twelve tribes, then picks up the narrative at Saul's death and stays with one king, David. It follows him as he is made king at Hebron, takes Jerusalem, brings the ark of God up to it, hears God's promise of a lasting house, and spends his last years gathering gold, workers and Levite singers for a Temple his son Solomon will build.

Much of the book is copied from Samuel, sometimes word for word, and the changes are the best clue to its purpose. Bathsheba, Uriah and Absalom's revolt are missing. The ark, the Levites and the Temple plans fill whole chapters. Written for Jews back from exile in Babylon, Chronicles tells them that God's promise to David and the worship of his house in Jerusalem still stand.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): Ezra wrote Chronicles. Most scholars today speak of an unnamed "Chronicler," probably a Levite or Temple writer in Jerusalem, and many think the books of Ezra and Nehemiah come from a different hand.

Written after the return from exile: most scholars say about 400–300 BC; some date it as early as 520 BC or as late as about 250 BC. The genealogy of David's line in 3:17–24 runs several generations past the exile. The story itself runs from Adam to David's death, about 970 BC.
Jerusalem and the land of Israel, seen from the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) after the exile.
Genealogies and lists (chapters 1–9; 23–27), historical narrative largely drawn from Samuel, a psalm made from Psalms 105, 96 and 106 (16:8–36), and speeches and prayers (17; 28–29).
Late Biblical Hebrew, with spellings and words of the Persian period.

29 chapters, 942 verses. 1 and 2 Chronicles were one book in Hebrew, Divre ha-Yamim, "the events of the days." The Greek calls it Paraleipomena, "things left out"; Jerome suggested the name "Chronicle." In the Hebrew Bible it usually stands last.

audience.to: The Jews of the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) and its Temple in Jerusalem, probably in the late Persian or early Greek period (about 400–300 BC). They were the descendants of exiles who had come back from Babylon, with some who had never left. They had a rebuilt Temple, priests and Levites, but no king of David's line. A governor appointed by Persia ruled a small territory around Jerusalem, and they had neighbors in Samaria and elsewhere who also claimed to be Israel.
audience.why: To tell this community who they were and what still stood. The genealogies (1–9) set them inside 'all Israel,' all twelve tribes, from Adam down to the people living in Jerusalem after the exile (9:1–34). The story of David then shows that the LORD's promise to David's house (17) was still valid. So was the worship David ordered, with its priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers (15–16; 23–26). Knowing the readers changes the reading. David's speeches and prayers are addressed to a king's assembly, but they are written to be heard by a later assembly with no king. Their message is: seek the LORD, give freely to his house, keep his law, and trust his promise. The book's silence about David's sins with Bathsheba is not ignorance, since its readers knew Samuel. It is a choice to hold up David as the founder of their worship.
views: Traditional readers, following the Talmud (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), hold that Ezra compiled Chronicles about 450–400 BC for the community he led. It taught them their history, its genealogies and the right order of worship.
The late Persian or early Greek period

Most scholars today, such as Japhet, Williamson and Knoppers, date the book about 400–300 BC. They see its first readers as a Temple community in Yehud, settled under Persian rule. These readers needed their identity as 'all Israel' and their worship tied to David.
A few scholars placed a first edition about 520–515 BC (Cross about 520, Freedman about 515). It was meant to support the building of the second Temple and the hopes around Zerubbabel, David's heir.
Some date it as late as about 250 BC, for a community living under the Ptolemies of Egypt.
Hope for David's line, or not

Williamson and others read the promise to David as a living hope for a future king. Others think the Chronicler had made peace with foreign rule and saw the Temple and its worship as the lasting form of David's kingdom.
Open or closed toward the north
Older scholars read Chronicles as aimed against the Samaritans. Since Williamson's Israel in the Books of Chronicles, most see a book that invites northerners back into 'all Israel' around Jerusalem.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Chronicles is a faithful second history, drawn from Samuel–Kings and from other records it names, such as the words of Samuel, Nathan and Gad (29:29). The Talmud names Ezra as its writer (Bava Batra 15a), and the Hebrew Bible places it last, as a summary of the whole story.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars date Chronicles to the Persian or early Greek period (about 400–250 BC) and read it as a deliberate rewriting of Samuel–Kings for the returned community in Judah, centered on the Temple, the Levites and David's line. They debate how far its extra material rests on older sources and how far it reflects the writer's own time.

lenses.name: Beside Samuel–Kings
lenses.desc: Chronicles copies, trims and adds to Samuel and Kings, and the changes are the clearest window into its purpose: David's sin with Bathsheba is left out, the ark and the Temple plans are expanded, and Satan, not the LORD, incites the census (21:1). Its Samuel text often agrees with the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a against the Masoretic Samuel.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis prize Chronicles for its genealogies and its picture of Temple worship, and read its names as a store of hidden lessons ('Chronicles was given only to be interpreted', Leviticus Rabbah 1:3). It closes the Hebrew Bible with the call to go up to Jerusalem.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus follows the lines in 1 Chronicles 1–3, and the promise of a son whose throne God will establish forever (17:11–14) is read as fulfilled in Christ. The Greek title, Paraleipomena ('things left out'), shows the early church read it as a supplement to Kings.

authorship: The Talmud says that "Ezra wrote his book and the genealogy of Chronicles up to his own time" (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), and that Nehemiah finished it. Many traditional Jewish and Christian readers have held that Ezra, a priest and scribe who returned to Jerusalem about 458 BC (Ezra 7:1–10), compiled Chronicles from Samuel–Kings and from the prophets' records it names, such as the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the visionary (29:29). The shared ending and beginning of 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 and Ezra 1:1–3 fit this view.

Most scholars speak of "the Chronicler," an unnamed writer, probably a Levite connected with the Temple in Jerusalem. They date the work to the late Persian or early Greek period, about 400–300 BC. The reasons are the late Hebrew, the coins called darics (29:7), and David's line running several generations past Zerubbabel (3:19–24). For a century after Leopold Zunz (1832), scholars thought one writer produced Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah as a single "Chronicler's history" (Curtis and Madsen; Martin Noth). Since Sara Japhet (1968) and H. G. M. Williamson (1977) compared their language and ideas, most think Ezra–Nehemiah comes from a different hand. Others still defend a common author or school.

Chronicles cites more than a dozen sources: the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, and records of prophets and seers. Scholars debate whether these were separate works, other names for Samuel–Kings, or a literary device. Many think the Chronicler did have some old lists, such as those of David's warriors and officials. Some also see later additions in the Levite lists of chapters 23–27.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site: YHWH is "the LORD"; YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (11:9); hesed is "loyal love" (16:34; 17:13); ma'al is "unfaithfulness" (10:13); nagid is "ruler" (11:2); and chozeh is "visionary."

Parallel passages

About a third of 1 Chronicles has a twin in Genesis, Samuel or Psalms. Where the Hebrew of Chronicles is the same as its parallel, the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording of that parallel exactly, so that a reader comparing the two sees only the real differences. Where the Hebrew differs, the English differs too, and a note or variant says whether the difference is Chronicles' own change, a different text of Samuel such as the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a or the Greek, or a copying slip. The psalm in 16:8–36 is translated from its own Hebrew; it will be aligned with the site's Psalms 105, 96 and 106 when those are written.

The text

The Hebrew of Chronicles is generally well preserved, but its names and numbers suffered in copying, and its Masoretic notes correct the written text in several places (11:11; 11:20; 14:1; 20:5). The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex except where a variant explains otherwise, as at 18:16. The Greek translation, called Paraleipomena, is close to the Hebrew and sometimes helps with names.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has three parts. Chapters 1–9 are genealogies: from Adam through the nations to Israel's twelve tribes, with Judah and David's line first, Levi in the center and Benjamin and Saul last. They end with the people who returned to Jerusalem after the exile (9:1–34). Chapters 10–21 tell David's reign: Saul's fall (10), David made king by all Israel (11–12), the ark brought to Jerusalem (13–16), God's promise (17), the wars (18–20), and the census that led to the Temple site (21). Chapters 22–29 describe David's preparations: materials, the organization of priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and officials, the plan of the Temple, and the handing over of the kingdom to Solomon.

Read as a whole, the book moves from people to place. First comes who Israel is, then where and how it worships. 2 Chronicles continues with Solomon's Temple and the kings of Judah, and it ends with Cyrus's call to go up and rebuild.

Readers have judged Chronicles very differently. In the nineteenth century W. M. L. de Wette and Julius Wellhausen argued that it was a late rewriting of Samuel–Kings, of little worth as history, which projected the Temple worship of its own day back onto David. Many critical scholars still see much of its added material, especially the Levite lists and the large numbers, as reflecting the Second Temple period.

Since the mid twentieth century, opinion has become more mixed. The Dead Sea scrolls showed that many differences from Samuel go back to a different Hebrew text of Samuel, not to the Chronicler's pen (Werner Lemke; Eugene Ulrich; Steven McKenzie). Scholars such as Sara Japhet, H. G. M. Williamson and Gary Knoppers describe the Chronicler as a real historian with strong convictions. He chose, arranged and explained his sources, but he did not simply invent. A minority view, argued by A. Graeme Auld, holds that Chronicles did not copy Samuel–Kings at all: both books drew on an older shared story of David's house, and each added to it. Some lists, such as David's officials and warriors, may preserve old records. Traditional readers take the book as reliable throughout and explain its differences from Samuel as selection, explanation and copying slips. The site presents these views side by side in the notes, under the lenses History as told, Critical and Beside Samuel–Kings.

Chronicles passes over the seven years of civil war at Hebron, David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah (compare 20:1 with 2 Samuel 11:1), Amnon and Tamar, Absalom's revolt, Sheba's rebellion and Adonijah's bid for the throne. Readers explain the silence in three main ways.

An idealized David. Wellhausen and many since have argued that the Chronicler cleaned up the image of David and Solomon for a community that looked to David's line, keeping what honored them and dropping what shamed them.

A focused history. Japhet, Williamson and others answer that Chronicles assumes its readers know Samuel and tells David's reign for one purpose, his founding of Israel's worship and his preparation for the Temple. On this view, the private troubles of his house did not serve that purpose. Chronicles keeps the census (21), David's own sin, because it led to the Temple site. It even says David's wars disqualified him from building the Temple (22:8). It also leaves out things that honor David, such as his lament for Saul and Jonathan and his kindness to Mephibosheth.

A model king. Others read the Chronicler's David and Solomon as a pattern of what the coming king and the faithful community should be. The portrait points forward more than back, and it is shaped by repentance and forgiveness rather than by denial.

All three views agree that the first readers knew the stories that Chronicles does not tell.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 1 Chronicles
sections.b:
In Jewish tradition Chronicles belongs to the Writings. The Talmud places it last in the Hebrew Bible (Bavli Bava Batra 14b), so that the Bible ends with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem; the Leningrad and Aleppo codices place it first in the Writings. The rabbis said, "Chronicles was given only to be interpreted" (Leviticus Rabbah 1:3), and they read its lists of names as a store of hidden lessons. Its song of thanks (16:8–36) is recited every morning in the synagogue service.

The Greek Bible placed Chronicles after Kings, under the title Paraleipomena, "things left out," and many Christians read it as a supplement to Kings. Jerome called it a summary of the whole Old Testament. Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Jesus draw on its lists. The New Testament reads the promise of 17:11–14, God's father-son bond with David's heir and a kingdom without end, as fulfilled in Christ (Luke 1:32–33; Hebrews 1:5). Christian churches have also drawn on its picture of ordered, joyful worship with singers and instruments.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book of gatherings
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: 1 Chronicles is built around gatherings of all Israel. The genealogies gather every tribe onto one page (1–9). Then all Israel gathers at Hebron to make David king (11:1; 12:38). The assembly gathers "from Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath" to bring up the ark (13:5), and again for the ark's arrival (15:3). David's last acts are two great assemblies of leaders and people (28:1; 29:1–20). The psalm at the center of the book ends with a prayer to be gathered from the nations (16:35). I suggest the Chronicler wrote for a scattered people, few in number and living under foreign rule. He showed them, again and again, an Israel gathered whole around God's king and God's house, as a picture of what God could do again. Scholars such as Williamson have stressed the "all Israel" theme in Chronicles; reading the book's structure as a series of gatherings is my own proposal.

prompts: The ark carried up to Jerusalem (15:25–28)

A long procession climbs a stony hill road toward a walled city on a ridge. In the center, four Levites in white linen carry a gold-covered chest on two long poles resting on their shoulders, two winged figures on its lid. Ahead of them, singers with bronze cymbals and men with lyres and harps; behind, priests blowing long silver trumpets. A bearded king in a plain linen robe dances in front of the ark with his arms raised. Crowds line the road, and from a window in the city wall a woman looks down.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.
David's warriors pour out the water of Bethlehem (11:17–19)

Inside a dark cave mouth at dusk, a bearded young king stands holding a clay water jar tipped downward, the water falling in a thin stream onto the rocky ground. Three tired warriors in short tunics with swords and dust on their legs stand before him, heads bowed. In the distance, through the cave mouth, the low walls of a small hill town and the tents of an enemy camp around a well.

A great branching tree drawn across the scroll, its roots marked by a single man and woman, its trunk splitting into twelve main branches, each hung with many small leaf shapes like names. One branch, thicker than the rest, rises to a small crown near the top; another holds a tiny temple. At the top right the branches bend toward a walled city on a hill, and a line of small figures with bundles walks toward it.

reading: Sara Japhet, I and II Chronicles (Old Testament Library, 1993)
A major critical commentary by the scholar who changed the study of Chronicles, careful on its sources and its ideas.
H. G. M. Williamson, 1 and 2 Chronicles (New Century Bible, 1982)
A compact, balanced commentary, strong on the book's purpose and its relation to Samuel–Kings.
Gary N. Knoppers, I Chronicles (Anchor Bible, 2 vols., 2004)
The fullest modern commentary, with a new translation and detailed textual notes.
A detailed critical commentary, especially good on the Hebrew text and its versions.
Martin J. Selman, 1 Chronicles (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, 1994)
A short evangelical commentary that reads Chronicles as an interpretation of Israel's earlier history.
John C. Endres, William R. Millar and John Barclay Burns, eds., Chronicles and Its Synoptic Parallels (1998)
Chronicles printed side by side with Samuel, Kings and the other parallels in English.
